draft.title: First Nations partnerships and cooperatives
card: a business owned by two or more people or groups who agree to share the work, the costs and the profits.
a business owned and run by its members, who pool their effort or money and share the benefits. Each member usually has an equal say.
Many First Nations businesses choose these forms. By sharing resources such as land, equipment, skills and money, a small business can do more than it could alone.

Joining together can also help businesses reach bigger markets. A group of artists or farmers can supply more customers, and take on larger orders, than one person could. This happens in farming, fashion, design and tourism.
draft.remember: Sharing resources through a partnership or cooperative can help First Nations businesses reach bigger markets.

opts: A business owned and run by its members who share benefits
A business owned by one person who keeps all the profits
A business owned by investors who take no part in running it
A business run by the government to supply a public service
a.why: A cooperative is owned and run by its members, who pool their effort or money and share the benefits. A business with one owner is a sole trader, so it is not a cooperative.
a.clue: Think about who owns it and who shares the benefits.

b.q: Five artists in a remote community each make textile designs. They form a group, share one studio and printing equipment, and sell together to city stores. What is the main benefit of joining together?
opts: They share resources and can supply larger orders
They no longer need to make any products themselves
They each gain full control over what the others make
They avoid all costs of running a business
b.why: Sharing a studio and equipment cuts what each artist must provide, and together they can fill bigger orders for city stores. They still make products and still have costs, so the other options are wrong.
b.clue: What does the group have that one artist alone would lack?

a.best: A business owned and run by its members who share benefits

b.best: They share resources and can supply larger orders

problems.detail: Every wrong option uses an absolute word ('all', 'full', 'any'), and only the right option is moderate and echoes the card's wording. A student could pick it by elimination without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card, the remember line and question a are accurate and stay on this point. In question b, the wrong options are all obvious extremes ('all', 'full', 'any'), so the right answer stands out; consider making them more plausible.
